newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine bill could mean debt, not jobs - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Argentine bill could mean debt, not jobs - analysts.

text.p: Powerful members of Argentina's governing Peronist Party plan to introduce a bill in Congress to create 600,000 jobs, but analysts fear the measure may create more debt than work.
Peronist Chamber of Deputies chief Jorge Matzkin is one of the sponsors of the bill, which calls for the creation of a trust fund to be financed by a Central Bank bond issue.
Peronist spokesmen said the bill will be introduced in Congress within two weeks, A copy of the draft bill was obtained by Reuters.
The bill does not give figures, but co-sponsor Congressman Oscar Lamberto said it would aim to create 600,000 jobs after raising $1.2 billion from bonds.

The bonds would be guaranteed by deferred tax payments owed by companies benefitting from industrial promotion measures. The government would subsidize job creation by paying firms $200 a month for each new employee.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Raul Buonuome expressed skepticism, saying Argentina will only really begin to reduce its 17.3-percent unemployment rate by pushing through long-delayed reforms to make labor contracts more flexible and cut employment costs.
"I don't know if the way to solve the problem is by subsidizing private companies," he told Reuters. "I think the way to solve the problem is labor reform."

With protests by the jobless a regular occurrence in the provinces, and President Carlos Menem's government assailed by corruption scandals, Peronists are focusing on unemployment before October's mid-term elections.

While the jobs plan would mean the government taking on $1.2 billion in new debt, it would not necessarily endanger Argentina's budget targets pledged to the International Monetary Fund, according to debt specialist Dolores Lopez Larroy, also of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Nor would it necessarily put strain on the "Convertibility Plan" pegging the peso at par with the dollar, she said.
"As the debt would be backed by future income of differed tax payments, it would be computed off-budget," Lopez said.
She added that world markets have proven to be hungry for Argentine bonds.
But Jose Luis Espert, Econometrica's chief economist, criticized the plan and said it would be illegal because the Central Bank's charter forbids it from issuing debt to fund public spending.
"The Economy Ministry wouldn't allow it anyway," he said.
